title: A practice plan
goal: Knowing the outlines is half of it. Speed comes from short, daily, honest practice on the words you miss.

items: **Lessons 2 to 7 first.** Do the drills until they pass cleanly twice. Slow and right beats fast and wrong.
**Lesson 8 in slices.** Ten common words a session, then mixed practice. These words are most of what you type.
**Lessons 10 to 13 by use.** Learn an ending when you want it. You do not need to memorise the whole table.
**Lessons 14 to 16 last.** Phrases, punctuation and letters pay off once words are fluent.
**Ten to twenty minutes**, once a day, beats an hour once a week.
Start with what you passed yesterday (Practice, mixed).
Then new material: one drill, or ten words.
End with **your misses**: Practice has a button that drills the words you keep getting wrong.

blocks.x: When you are stuck on a word

items: **Lookup** shows the fastest outline and the other ways in.
No one-stroke form? Say it, split it, join the syllables (lesson 12).
Always hold the join key on every stroke after the first.

blocks.x: These drills read an ordinary keyboard. Once the outlines are in your hands, move to a steno keyboard or a keyboard mapper with the generated dictionary (see the main README for building it), and practise on text you actually want to write.

Real use will show you the words you want a shorter form for. That is the point of the theory: it is a dictionary generated by rules, so your most common words can be given the cheapest strokes without losing the rule underneath.

These lessons condense the chapters in the [docs folder](https://github.com/noahlyk/lyk-steno-theory/tree/main/docs). Read them when you want the reasoning: why a stroke is what it is, how collisions are settled, what each choice cost.
